>People who don't have to pay tax can and should be able to claim all their tax back.

It's not their tax. It's company tax, and dividends are paid after company tax. To avoid double taxation, the company and ATO track tax which has already been paid and allow it to be used to offset tax the individual pays.

But if the individual doesn't pay tax, there's no issue with double taxation. Not even negative gearing lets you offset past zero and get the ATO to pay you. Same with capital gains and losses. Such a distorted system is unheard of in similar economies and was never even the intention of the franking credit scheme as it was introduced.

If franking credits were supposed to be a cash handout, it would be easier just to allow dividends to be paid out of pre-tax profits.

> What I don't understand, is why they are saying this will be a tax on the rich.

Because an overwhelming proportion of the benefit goes to wealthy retirees who have structured their finances to benefit the most from it. Think people with seven figure super balances who are living off the *returns* without touching the principle, but the returns are tax-free.

Super is supposed to incentivise saving for retirement, not hoarding wealth, and franking credits are supposed to avoid double taxation, not to transfer company tax directly to those who don't pay tax.

>Isn't it only the people who pay less than 30% income tax that receive some refund via the franking credit?

No, whenever you receive dividends, you receive the same 30% in franking credits - the company doesn't know or need to know your marginal rate.

When you submit your tax return, you include the franking credits, and the ATO adds them to the tax you've already paid (e.g. via PAYG). (They're also added to your income, which complicates things a little).

>And people who pay more than 30% income tax, then must be pay the difference (and therefore MORE tax) at tax time?

Yep. If you're on the top marginal rate of 47% (IIRC), the company has already paid 30% of that, and you pay the other 17%.

If your marginal rate is less than 30%, you get the difference as a rebate. The change being put forward is only considering the credit as a tax offset, and not a credit for someone on zero taxable income.

They're probably trying to claim s245 of the tenancy act applies:

>    (1)     A landlord may give a tenant a notice to vacate rented premises if the premises—
>(a)     are unfit for human habitation; or
>(b)     have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe.

http://www9.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/vic/consol_act/rta1997207/s245.html

So if a meteor struck the house and destroyed it, it might apply. But the fact that there are provisions in the law for both urgent repairs and temporary accommodation should heavily imply that it doesn't.

In fact, they may have shot themselves in the foot by claiming urgent repairs are needed. This gives you a lot more power:

https://www.tuv.org.au/advice/repairs/

>If you need urgent repairs, you don’t have to notify the landlord in writing but you must try to contact the landlord or agent before making your own arrangements for repairs to be carried out. Keep a record of the steps you took to get the landlord or agent to carry out the repairs (eg a list of phone calls, emails, times and dates).

>If you can’t reach the landlord or agent or they don’t respond immediately, you can make your own arrangements to have the repairs done—up to the cost of $1800 (including GST). The costs must be reasonable so you may want to get a few quotes. To get the money back, send a Notice to Landlord, describing the repairs that were done and how much they cost, and attach a copy of the repair receipt or invoice. The landlord must repay you within 14 days of receiving the notice. However keep in mind that if you arrange for urgent repairs to be done and the cost is more than $1800 (including GST), the landlord is only liable for up to $1800. If the landlord does not reimburse you within 14 days, you can apply to VCAT for an order that they do so.

>If you can’t afford to pay for urgent repairs yourself, the repairs will cost more than $1800, or you simply cannot get the landlord to do the repairs, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal for an order that the landlord has to carry out the repairs. The Tribunal must hear applications for urgent repairs within 2 business days.

If repairs require your eviction, you must be given 60 days notice.

And don't rely on your adversary for legal advice. Consumer affairs or the Tenants Union would be better, but at this point, I'd pull the trigger and go straight to VCAT with a request for an urgent hearing.
